summary: Describes the de facto Digest Message Format, a way of bundling many mail messages into one message, as used by mailing lists. It is an elective experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: Instead of getting every letter on its own, you get one big envelope with many letters inside.

subtitle: The standard format for bundling multiple email messages into a single digest.

tldr.problem: High-traffic mailing lists needed a way to reduce overhead by bundling multiple messages into one, while preserving message headers and allowing reconstruction of individual messages.
tldr.mechanism: The digest format wraps several complete messages (each with its own header and body) inside a single RFC 822 message, separated by delimiter lines, with a preamble table of contents and a closing trailer.
tldr.outcome: A de facto standard format emerged that allowed mailing list digestification and was documented for interoperability.

facts.label: Header retention fields
facts.value: Date, From, To, Cc, Subject, Message-ID, Keywords

today: RFC 1153 is an Experimental Internet Standard describing a de facto standard format that has been in continuous use for mailing list digests since the 1970s.

sections.title: Why Digests Exist
sections.content: High-traffic large mailing lists began appearing on the internet in the mid-1970s. Mailing list moderators developed digest messages as a way to reduce network overhead and mail server load. By bundling many messages into one composite message, bandwidth is conserved and mailer load is proportional to the number of digests rather than the number of individual messages. The digest format became the de facto standard for this purpose, predating RFC 934's generic message encapsulation and remaining the preferred format for digest messages.
sections.eli5: When many people email a group, the mail system gets overwhelmed. Putting all the emails together into one big message uses less electricity and is faster for everyone.

sections.title: The Digest Structure
sections.content: A digest message conforms to RFC 822 (the standard for internet mail) and has no fixed size, though intermediate mail gateways may impose limits. The typical digest is around 15,000 characters. The digest header should identify the digest in the Subject line by listing the mailing list name, the word "Digest", a volume number, and an issue number. The message body must consist of three parts: a Preamble containing a table of contents and administrative announcements, one or more enclosed messages, and a Trailer marking the end. Each enclosed message retains specific header lines in a defined order (Date, From, To, Cc, Subject, Message-ID, Keywords), and removes Received lines and other extraneous headers. Messages are separated by blank lines and a line of exactly 30 hyphens.
sections.eli5: The big envelope has a table of contents at the top, then each letter inside, each separated by a line of dashes, and at the very end a note saying this is the end of the digest.

sections.title: Reconstructing Individual Messages
sections.content: The digest format allows moderators to edit content and reformat messages while preserving the essential message structure needed for reconstruction. Software can separate (undigestify) the composite message back into individual messages by identifying the separator lines and extracting each enclosed message. By retaining the key header fields and removing only Received lines and blank lines, the original message context is preserved. The format also allows optional replacement of lines of exactly 30 hyphens in message bodies with a blank character to prevent false matches with the message separator delimiter.
sections.eli5: The format makes it easy to take the big envelope apart again into separate emails. The important information from each letter is kept so the undigestifier software can put them back together.
